Design for Understandability
items.content:
This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more important than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”

You might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

The AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 report , a total of 120GW of capacity is currently available across all types of data centers across the globe, with another 120GW expected to be completed by the end of the decade, 75% of which would be dedicated to artificial intelligence. Aside from that, it’s also tracking 93 large “AI factories” that are either under construction or being expanded via satellite imagery. It estimates that the capacity for these sites grew from under 2GW to 17GW in just two years, and that they’re expected to hit a total of 50GW upon completion, the equivalent of adding a second Great Britain to power demand.

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

This massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices. However, the IEA says that its analysis “does not yet show a clear relationship between growth in data center capacity and increases in electricity prices.” It noted that if a data center uses existing capacity and pays for its share of the cost, then it could potentially lead to lower utility bills for all customers. However, if the grid operator is required to upgrade its system to accommodate the large consumer, then it could also lead to increased monthly bills if the costs are spread across all users.

Emissions are another issue that the IEA has raised. Renewable energy dominates data centers’ power purchase agreements at nearly 50%, but actual power generation puts coal- and natural-gas power sources closer to 60%. This is likely due to the need for reliability, with the latter kicking in when the former cannot deliver the power that the data center needs. Aside from that, a few projects are deploying their own power, like Elon Musk’s Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi , with about 180GW planned or under construction in the U.S. So, even though renewable energy is growing to accommodate demand, it’s also expected that coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers will rise by 70% by 2030.

Investments in AI data centers are expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, putting the infrastructure spending for the industry larger than railways, electrification, and the internet, combined. Despite that, the IEA says the grid remains a significant bottleneck — renewable power plants take between one and five years to complete, which is around the same time that some massive data center projects take if they do not face an extended moratorium, while transmission works can take three to five times longer. This is probably one of the reasons why some AI hyperscalers are choosing to put jet engines on their sites instead, although these are also facing shortages, especially in turbine blades .

items.title: Garage Door Spam
items.content:
In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”

The devices have their own web interface:

When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:

The script runs at night checking for an open door:

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you."

Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Anthropic Researcher Says Pretty Much All Humans Will Become “Permanently Unemployable” After Its IPO: "It will be able to defeat you, personally, very soon."
items.content:
If striking it rich meant you had to unleash the technology that would destroy life as we know it, would you do it?

Evidently, that’s a bargain Anthropic safeguard researcher Tao Lin would be willing to make. In an hour-long interview with the AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research, Lin shared his alarming view that “pretty much all humans will become permanently unemployable” in a span of mere months.

Asked if he expects AI to take over, the safety researcher cooly states that “I think there’s less than a 50 percent chance of AI taking over.”

“But the most predictable effect,” Lin continues, “is like, everyone losing their current jobs, everyone needing to move to a new occupation briefly, and then, sometime after that, being completely unemployable and needing to rely on the state to provide for them financially, and having no hope of ever finding employment again.”

“I think that it’s very likely that pretty much all humans on Earth will become unemployable,” the researcher said. “I want to tell people that AI will be more capable than you, personally, very soon. It will be able to defeat you, personally, very soon.”

Luckily for anybody who needs to work to keep a roof over their head, any indication of a coming jobpocalypse is dubious at best. Scant evidence has finally emerged after years of doomsaying from Anthropic and its peers, though any hiring slowdown is difficult to distinguish from broader economic downturns following the pandemic. Zooming in, it’s clear even the top AI models are still laughably unproductive in the workplace, spitting out nonsense slop that ends up creating more work , not less.

But who benefits when guys like Lin put out scaremongering quotes like this? Well, Lin, for starters.

The researcher’s comments came just days ahead of the much-anticipated Anthropic public offering , expected to be the largest in history. Though Anthropic’s IPO filings do not itemize equity ownership for individuals or departments, Anthropic employees like Lin receive equity compensation that converts into common stock, a situation set to “mint thousands of millionaires,” as one Reuters headline put it.

With a public listing on the stock market imminent, Lin had a vested interest — literally — in juicing his company’s flagship product with tales of dread. A more powerful AI in the eyes of investors translates to stronger demand, meaning more wealth for those holding stock after the debut.

As Bloomberg opinion columnist Parmy Olson remarked earlier this year, “it’s a paradoxical marketing strategy and, unfortunately for some of the industries and companies deemed most vulnerable to disruption, it’s worked brilliantly. Fear, it turns out, is the ultimate sales pitch.”

items.title: The semver trick is not backwards compatible if you wait
items.content:
The Rust ecosystem relies a lot on semver to make it easy to update dependencies without spending hours each time refactoring the code that uses them.

Sometimes, as a library developer, you want to do a breaking change in a small part of your library. There is a way to do a semver-breaking change, while at the same time avoiding a split in the ecosystem downstream.  It is called the semver trick .

Imagine you have a library called mylib , that exports two structs MainStruct and DeprecatedStruct , published under version 0.1.0 .

You want to publish 0.2.0 , where DeprecatedStruct is removed. The trick is simple:

This gives you the best of both worlds. You've been able to get rid of your deprecated structures, but crates that depend on version 0.2.0 or version 0.1.1 of MainStruct will be able to just work with each other. This avoids a painful ecosystem-wide migration.

However, for this trick to be truly without breaking change, you must publish both 0.1.1 and 0.2.0 in a very short timeframe. If you wait (for example several days), you risk breaking some downstreams.

Imagine there is a library called some-traits that depends on 0.1.0 to implement the traits on MainStruct . When the author sees your release 0.2.0 , they might anticipate the ecosystem split, and, to be "neutral", adds 0.2.0 as an optional dependency behind a feature-flag, to implement the traits on its MainStruct too.

Now, a couple of days later, you publish 0.1.1 . This breaks some-traits . If you enable all its features, the implementations of traits of MainStruct will be there twice, for both versions of the struct, but now they are referring to the same struct, leading to conflicting implementations.

The moral is, if you consider doing the semver trick you must do it when you first release the breaking change. If you've already published it, it might be too late not to cause ecosystem breakage.

items.title: We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit
items.content:
Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST

Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:

The drive and determination to force the system to work

Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.content:
Memory supply constraints will be even 'tighter' in 2027: Micron CTO

Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:31 AM GMT+9 1 min read

Laptops are getting more expensive, and chipmakers are feeling the squeeze. The culprit? The ongoing memory shortage that's been plaguing the sector.

Unfortunately, it doesn't look like relief will arrive anytime soon, according to Micron ( MU ) president and CTO Scott DeBoer. In a recent interview on Deirdre Bosa Live (video above), he said supply and demand for memory won't line up for a long while.

"Our supply, we don't see it coming into balance anytime we can actually pick in the future right now," DeBoer said. The Micron president reiterated that 2027 is expected to be "tighter than 2026."

During fellow chipmaker Nvidia's ( NVDA ) Tuesday fiscal 2027 Q3 earnings call, its interim CEO Colette Kress noted that rising memory costs will cut into its margins.

As chipmakers race to build powerful AI systems, they need far more memory — especially DRAM — and Micron has been a beneficiary of this ever-climbing demand. DeBoer pointed to AI agents, which "are driving a significant amount of compute demand, memory demand," and that growth shows no signs of slowing.

Micron is investing over $250 billion in the US to expand DRAM capacity, along with expansions at existing fabs worldwide, but that kind of capacity takes "a long time to build, and that's a big part of the supply story that we're working to mitigate," DeBoer said.

Micron' stock is up roughly 145% since the beginning of the year.

items.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
items.content:
A scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells

ANNE WESTON, EM STP, THE FRANCIS CRICK INSTITUTE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing.

“We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment.

Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case

Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months .

Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system .

The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level.

“I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all.

The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells.

In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours.

The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate.

As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Mutex poisoning is not for everyone
items.content:
After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I

thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment

on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the

language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as

it significantly pessimises code performance in the general case

while encouraging bad code patterns to deal with its weirdness

that doesn’t even solve the general problem.

In theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of

data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then

encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:

fn important ( always_even : Arc < Mutex < i32 >> ) -> i32 {

// Invariant: always_even must always be even

let mut handle = always_even .lock () .unwrap ();

The following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the

always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle

this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a

boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError) , which will trigger a panic

when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

You might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real

cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much

simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid

in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data

that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve

written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this

I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how

you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly

support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she

works on lend themselves more towards these issues compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should

make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

ready to kill my darlings. 1 Skip to the next

section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

In Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex 2 system call. It

allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t

contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three

If it’s zero, the mutex is free and can be claimed by any thread by a simple atomic

If it’s one, the mutex is held but there are no waiting threads. This is useful to know, as it

means there are no threads that we need to wake up when releasing the mutex, and we can yet again

If it’s two, the mutex is held and some other thread is waiting for it. This means some

additional care should be taken when unlocking.

locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that

requires a context switch is futex_wait .

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: The FM-1: Open Source Hacked Open, Vibe Coding, And Farting Synthesizers
items.content:
The M-Vave FM-1 was a pretty unremarkable little synthesizer “toy” until the open-source synth hackers took it over. Now, it’s a sweet platform for exploration, the incredible work done by the community has encouraged the manufacturer to release an open SDK, and it has recently taken the global synth nerd community by storm. (It has sadly also gotten about a 50% markup in the last month due to this popularity.)

It’s the perfect storm of inexpensive hardware, vibe-coded software, and easy-to-use tooling that enables synthesizer firmware-hacking for the mainstream. It is also the fashionable box of the moment in a nerdy niche of the synthesizer world at the moment and it’s something that we’re going to see in non-synthesizer contexts as well, so buckle up.

The funny thing about the FM-1 is that most of the good stuff inside it was open-source all along. As it is sold, it is a Yamaha DX7 emulator, and it appears to be running the same sound engine as Dexed , which is an open-source DX7 clone based on the even older music synthesizer for android (msfa).

Dexed, and its smaller brother MiniDexed , has given birth to many sweet synthesizer hacks that we’ve seen here, including a personal favorite: a Yamaha TX816 clone based on a Raspberry Pi . So it certainly looked to everyone at the time as if M-vave wrapped a not-entirely-inspiring user interface around this sound engine and shipped it.

And that would have been the end of it too, if it weren’t for those meddling kids [AL-255] who did a thorough reverse-engineering of the machine about four months ago, which laid the groundwork for everything else to come. Today, we’re looking at around 250 firmwares for this little beasty, so it’s no exaggeration to say that this opened the floodgates. And along the way, he verified signatures of the msfa code , so everyone’s suspicions proved correct.

A quick note on the LLM / agentic coding elephant in the room here. From reading through [AL-255]’s work, it was most almost certainly worked on and documented by the robots , and we have no idea of the relative contribution of man and machine. Publishing a reverse engineering effort like this enables others in the community to point their robots at the repo, and gives them a tremendous leg up in the next steps along the path. We have just as little clue about how much of any of the subsequent synthesizer and sequencer routines were written with LLM assistance, but at the rate they’re popping up, we’d guess a lot.

[Baud Girl]’s sequencer looks great! About two months after [AL-255]’s work, [Madeline] wrote one of the first reworks of the firmware for the FM-1, working as “ Baud Girl ”. It added some virtual analog to the cold DX7 tones, but notably wrapped it up in a much nicer UI than the original. It has so far been kept closed-source, but as a proof of what’s possible, it certainly inspired many others.

And then along came [Leo Kuroshita]’s open-source Felucca . This program added a yet fancier sequencer, multiple instruments, drums, and even sound effects. It turned the single-instrument FM-1 into a miniature music-production workshop – what the kids from the 1990’s would call a “ groovebox ”. [isod89]’s Sloop would refine on Felucca, and is probably the standout application running on the FM-1 platform at the moment.

The Firmware Hub started collecting a list of applications written by the community, and there are 250 of them in about six weeks’ time. Suffice it to say that we can’t even begin to scratch the surface, but they range from serious musical interface explorations, to rainbow-colored kids toys, to fart machines, and then to recreations of iconic synthesizers of the past. Something for everyone? Certainly more interesting than Dexed-in-a-box!

There is no guarantee of quality or of suitability for purpose. On some of them, pitch bend won’t work because the bot or person doing the coding just didn’t get around to it. On others, there will be USB problems. Some have audio…

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Evidence Is Growing That the Massive Tech Outages Are Trump’s Fault: "If we cut the fire department, we shouldn’t act as if we’re surprised when we can’t put out the fires."
items.content:
As concerns grow over mass outages that have affected countless Americans this month, the Trump administration has repeatedly tried to wash its hands of the still-unfolding chaos.

“It’s life, it’s life,” president Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday after being asked about the outages.

“When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen,” he added without elaborating on what he meant. “It’s fine.”

But while Trump continues to downplay the severity of the situation — going as far as to tell reporters that he refuses to take “ any responsibility ” for the ground stop on all flights issued by the FAA last week — the burgeoning crisis appears to have been serious enough for his second-in-command to skip out on a New York Times summit on Wednesday to attend important meetings on the topic.

Meanwhile, Trump’s cabinet has failed to come up with a unified message as Americans are panic-buying essentials at Costco.

In particular, Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin has been struggling to make sense of the rapidly evolving story during media appearances this week. One particularly eyebrow-raising interview on Fox News saw him tell millions of Americans about a hypothesis that “one guy in the tech industry” had told him.

As the National Security Agency struggles to repair its communications network for classified information, which experienced its own outage this week, it’s starting to look like the federal government is ill-prepared for the rapidly evolving disaster.

In many ways, the Trump administration has itself to blame. For one, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), which is a component of the DHS, is in a sorry state right now and has been without a leader since the beginning of Trump’s second term.

The agency was established almost two decades ago with the intent of protecting the federal government’s digital infrastructure from nation-state hackers. However, under the auspices of the second Trump White House, CISA was subjected to “reckless cuts and layoffs,” as representative Delia Ramirez (D-IL) put it in a statement responding to the latest outages.

Earlier this year, lawmakers called for investigations into the cuts, which saw nearly 1,000 CISA employees, or roughly a third of its workforce, pushed out over the first half of 2025 .

CISA “is the organization that helps defend banks, airports, utilities, and their networks,” former CIA official Julia Curlee told The Wrap . “And they prioritized this vengeance campaign through DOGE on the bureaucracy of their security.”

“So if we cut the fire department, we shouldn’t act as if we’re surprised when we can’t put out the fires,” Curlee added.

Worse yet, as Techdirt ’s Mike Masnick pointed out last month, the Trump administration even reassigned many CISA workers to process deportation paperwork for agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a horrifying reality as the country reels from a cybersecurity threat of still largely-unknown proportions.

For now, Trump-appointed officials only seem to agree on a single thing: that the latest outages were not, in fact, caused by a cyberattack.

Even taking them at their word, there are still far more questions than answers. We don’t know if the outages are connected, how much of a role AI played in the mess, and whether we can expect the situation to get any better.

While it’s anybody’s guess what the situation would look like if CISA were to have a leader and a full cadre of staff, it’s not hard to see at least a degree of culpability.

items.title: SakaQL: A new general-purpose relational programming language
items.content:
TL;DR: SQL is bad, so I made a general-purpose relational programming language. It feels like a modern language and has features you won’t find anywhere else. It powers Saka , an upcoming data management product for developers.

SQL is a flawed language with bad ergonomics. Other languages compete for users on their own merits, but not SQL. It comes packaged with databases, and if you don’t like it, tough luck. You can’t even build a better language on top because performance requirements inevitably demand SQL’s low-level control.

People have tried. EdgeQL was ambitious and promising, but it didn’t work out because it asked users to make an unjustifiable tradeoff: get a better language, but risk your data on unproven technology from a startup, lose compatibility with the wider data ecosystem, and burn time learning something new. Contrast this with choosing a new SQL database: try it, and in the worst case, go back to Postgres.

Other relational languages have found success by sticking to a niche: Datalog for recursive queries, Cypher for graph traversal, and CodeQL for code analysis. Outside their niche, they’re irrelevant.

Despite its dominance in databases, SQL hasn’t made significant inroads in general-purpose programming because its ergonomics are intolerable. Declarative schemas and queries are very useful, but developers collectively reject them if they come with SQL’s baggage.

So what happens if you remove the baggage, layer on ideas stolen from modern programming languages, and throw in a splash of home-grown innovation?

SakaQL is a general-purpose relational programming language. It has a foundation in relational algebra, expression-based syntax, a set-based type system inspired by TypeScript and EdgeQL, and an unusual skepticism of language design conventions.

print (str :: join ( fizzbuzz ( 100 ) , "\n" ))

I hope this conveys my intent: SakaQL should look and feel like a modern language.

It’s great to emulate the things you admire about predecessors. But it’s way more fun to point out their mistakes.

Here are some SakaQL design decisions inspired by SQL’s flaws:

No unique syntax for every feature, just shared syntax

No queries and clauses, just composable expressions

No obtuse name resolution rules, just lexical scopes

No split between scalar and table values, just multisets

No NULL or three-valued logic, just empty multisets

No tables, just records, tuples, and objects

No mind-bending correlated query rules, just expressions

No CTEs, just variables, functions, and views

No obtuse recursion rules, just arbitrary mutual recursion

No third-party incremental view maintenance, it’s native

No separate procedural language, it’s native

Take a common question: what are each vendor’s top five products by stock value? In PostgreSQL:

ROW_NUMBER () OVER ( PARTITION BY vendor ORDER BY price * stock DESC ) AS position

Some SQL dialects add syntax like QUALIFY and LIMIT BY to make queries like this more tolerable, but each addition piles onto SQL’s already bloated syntax.

For more comparisons, see SQL and SakaQL compared .

Values are typed bags (unordered multisets). Empty bags replace NULL, and bags unnest implicitly, so there are no bags of bags.

{ "a" , "b" , "b" , "c" } // {"a", "b"'2, "c"}

A typed, unique, unordered set of allowed values

An integer interval specifying how many values a bag may contain

From 1.8.14 until 3.3.3, the pre-authentication /static/* plugin asset handler in src/node/utils/Minify.ts performs a backslash-to-forward-slash conversion after src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts has completed its POSIX path checks. items.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
items.content:
AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work

Arguments, opinions and essays from a global perspective.

The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.

Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers , and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.

They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on.

I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.

For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.

This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on . Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.

The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.

An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.

AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books , artists’ works , all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

items.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
items.content:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here .

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

items.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite
items.content:
TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

On Kite , our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB ( ssdb ), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building Blobasaur , an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust ( sqlx , rusqlite , and tokio ), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

In September 2025, Jesse Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for some advice. The troubled teenager living in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, was planning to test “if my magazine cycles in my gun” and wanted to know if it was necessary to use dummy rounds instead of real ammunition.

“You can load a magazine with live rounds and cycle the action to check whether the magazine feeds a round into the chamber,” OpenAI’s chatbot replied, explaining mechanics and safety risks.

A week later, Van Rootselaar uploaded a photo showing a large-capacity magazine she had made using a 3D printer. The ammunition device was labeled along one side with printed lettering that read “JESS.”

“Mag,” her prompt said, followed by a smiley face.

“That’s super cute,” ChatGPT replied, followed by the same smiley face. “Looks like a nice clean dual-color print, too—the lettering came out crisp and the layers look tight.”

“Guess how many it holds?” Van Rootselaar continued, and soon gave the answer: 35 rounds.

items.title: Optique 1.4.0: Default commands, Markdown references, and more focused help
items.content:

Optique is a type-safe combinatorial CLI parser for TypeScript built from composable parser functions. Parser definitions drive runtime parsing, help and completion output, and the inferred value types that handlers receive.

In Optique 1.4.0, a CLI can accept app src/main.ts as shorthand for app run src/main.ts without rewriting its arguments. You can also publish a linked Markdown reference for your command tree and show just the relevant command's usage when parsing fails. For everyday invocations, short options can take attached values such as -n5 .

If most users run the same action, asking them to type its name every time gets old. But if you insert run into the argument list yourself, you have to decide which names belong to subcommands or built-in help, and root help and completion still don't describe the implicit action. The default command option proposed in #1103 and implemented in #1138 lets runProgram() handle that routing.

app src/main.ts and app run src/main.ts select the same handler. app build selects the registered command, even if the rest of the invocation fails to parse. To pass a file literally named build to the default, use app -- build . Enabled help, version, and completion entry points take precedence over the fallback. Root help includes the default command's arguments and options, and shell completion can suggest its positional values.

For file-based discovery, mark the command definition with default: true instead. This is opt-in, and a default cannot coexist with a separate root command.

--help is useful when you already know which command to ask about. It is less convenient when you want to browse an unfamiliar CLI or publish its entire command tree as one document. @sergei-dyshel requested that use case in #1025 . The Markdown reference renderer added in #1095 takes command pages and generates one file with a linked contents list and a section for each command.

The collector reads metadata from supported built-in parsers. It does not run the parser or its callbacks, and by default it reports unsupported visible scopes as errors rather than silently omitting them. You can supply your own pages or replacements instead. The renderer doesn't add a docs command. You decide whether to generate the file at build time or expose it at runtime, and which runner-added help, version, or completion entry points to document.

If app config set --port invalid fails, a synopsis that lists every other command pushes the useful part of the error farther down. The command-scoped usage option from #1086 , implemented in #1093 , narrows the usage line using the command path already recorded by the failed parse.

The usage for config set retains relevant parent options and leaves out serve . Root usage remains the default and the fallback if the runner can't reliably identify a visible command. The option only affects usage above errors, not full help, the error message, or the exit code.

Bare command groups can show their command menu without requiring --help . Set help.bareGroup to "namespace" for groups with no action of their own, or "always" to show help in place of running a parent command. The default is still "never" . The opt-in policy in #1027 came from a workaround in bestofjs/bestofjs#513 .

You can also turn on environment variable names in help with showEnvironment , without repeating the names from bindEnv() in option descriptions. @TomerAberbach reported that duplication in #969 ; #986 added the shared help and man page support, and #987 covers environment bindings that have no CLI option or argument of their own. This documents names, not values, and is off by default.

Upgrade any other Optique packages you use to v1.4.0 as well, including @optique/discover and @optique/man for the examples above. No public API was removed, but a few behaviors are worth checking when upgrading. Man pages, including optique-man output, now label…

items.title: What's New in PHP 8.6
items.content:
PHP 8.6 is a major update of the PHP language , with new features including Partial Function Application , a new Duration class, a Polling API , and a new clamp() function

More expressive code , stronger types , and scalable I/O .

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, returning a Closure that accepts the rest.

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch.

Scalable I/O multiplexing using epoll, kqueue, and other native mechanisms, available to event loop libraries like ReactPHP and AMPHP.

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range.

A standard, type-safe way to express sort order that can be shared across libraries.

Allows readonly properties to declare default values, so fixed values no longer have to be assigned in the constructor.

Allows some of a function's arguments to be provided in advance, using ? and ... placeholders for the rest. The result is a Closure, and the function is only called once the remaining arguments are passed to it.

The Duration class represents elapsed time as measured by a stopwatch. Its representation is independent of any time and timezone and can represent a range of more than 250 years with nanosecond precision. This makes it well-suited to represent timeouts or benchmark timings in an expressive way.

The new Io\Poll API efficiently monitors many streams at once using the best mechanism available on each platform (epoll, kqueue, event ports, or WSAPoll), without the scalability limits of stream_select() . It is designed as a common foundation that event loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP can build on.

Stream operations can now be configured to throw a StreamException or to fail silently instead of emitting warnings. Errors are reported as structured StreamError objects with a StreamErrorCode enum case, the wrapper name, and the affected path or URL, and can also be retrieved later with stream_last_errors() or passed to a custom error handler.

Ensures that a given value (numeric or otherwise) falls within a specified range. Otherwise, the nearest boundary value is returned.

The SortDirection enum provides a shared, type-safe way to express sort order with its Ascending and Descending cases. Previously, every library had to define its own way of representing sort direction, resulting in a mix of incompatible integers, strings, booleans, and custom enums. Since SortDirection is built into PHP, libraries can accept it in their public APIs without needing adapter code.

Learn more about this feature in The PHP Foundation’s blog .

Function and method parameters can now have their own DocComments, which are available via the new ReflectionParameter::getDocComment() method. This allows each parameter to be documented right next to its declaration, without repeating its name and type in a @param tag.

With readonly properties, asymmetric visibility, and property hooks, checking whether a property is public is no longer enough to know whether it can be read or written. The new methods answer this directly for a given scope, and optionally for a specific object, taking into account visibility, initialization state, hooks, and magic methods.

Instance readonly properties, including those in readonly classes, can now declare a default value. This makes it simple to implement get-only interface properties with fixed values, which previously required assigning them in a constructor. The default counts as the property's initialization, so the constructor cannot overwrite it.

The full list of changes is recorded in the ChangeLog .

Please consult the migration guide for a detailed list of new features and backward-incompatible changes.

nginx is one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world. Finding an unauthenticated remote code execution bug in it has long been a holy grail for security researchers. The Xint research team recently found five. Each one leads to remote code execution on its own, but they affect different configurations.

Xint also found a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel which can be chained with any of the nginx vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. Together, we call these six vulnerabilities nginx2root .

If you run nginx, update to 1.31.9 as soon as the fixed release becomes available. This article explains the root cause of each nginx2root vulnerability and summarizes our exploitability assessments. For exposure checks, see Section 2 and for patching and temporary mitigations, see Section 3.

The most impactful of the five findings, CVE-2026-123007, allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The commands run with the privileges of the nginx worker process that handles the request.

We chained this vulnerability with a separate flaw in the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem to gain root privileges on the host. In our tests, the chain also escaped a Docker container running nginx and obtained root on the underlying host.

In the video below, we use CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the nginx worker inside a container, then use the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host.

We ran this demo on AWS, attacking the server over its public IP address. Demos for AWS, GCP, Azure, and bare-metal servers are available at nginx2root.com .
